C005.subject: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold
C005.object: the interaction of fire feedback intensity with belowground hydraulic redistribution, under conditions of moderate deforestation and normal drought cycles
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold the interaction of fire feedback intensity with belowground hydraulic redistribution, under conditions of moderate deforestation and normal drought cycles]

[PATH:empirical] Field-based manipulation experiments in the southern Amazon basin combining controlled fire treatments with measurements of soil moisture and root hydraulic redistribution (e.g., through isotopic tracing of deep water uptake by vegetation) — Directly tests how fire feedback intensity alters belowground hydraulic redistribution and whether this interaction shifts the forest toward a dieback threshold under moderate deforestation and normal drought cycles.

[PATH:theoretical] Process-based ecosystem model simulations (e.g., LPJ-GUESS, ED2, or CLM-FATES) that couple dynamic fire modules with explicit representations of hydraulic redistribution and are run under scenarios of moderate deforestation and historical drought variability for the 21st century — Provides a controlled virtual environment to isolate the interaction term and quantify its effect on dieback threshold, allowing comparison against models that omit hydraulic redistribution.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on Amazon forest resilience, focusing on studies that report fire frequency, tree mortality, and hydraulic traits (e.g., rooting depth, xylem vulnerability) across deforestation gradients in the southern and eastern Amazon — Synthesizes available empirical evidence to assess whether the hypothesized interaction is consistently associated with dieback events, and identifies data gaps for targeted field studies.

scope.domain: fire ecology and plant hydraulic dynamics interactions

qualifier.temporal: during the 21st century under projected moderate deforestation and normal drought cycles
qualifier.geographic: southern and eastern Amazon basin regions where fire feedback and hydraulic redistribution are most active

C006.subject: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold
C006.object: deforestation rates, regardless of fire feedback intensity and drought cycles
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold deforestation rates, regardless of fire feedback intensity and drought cycles]

[PATH:empirical] Long-term satellite-based deforestation and fire data (e.g., PRODES, DETER) combined with vegetation stress indices (e.g., EVI, NDVI) across the Brazilian Amazon from 2000 to present — Provides direct observational evidence to test whether deforestation rates alone predict dieback thresholds, controlling for fire feedback intensity and drought cycles via statistical or machine learning models.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic global vegetation model (DGVM) experiments isolating deforestation from fire and drought effects (e.g., LPJmL, INLAND, or CABLE-POP runs with factorial design) — Allows controlled simulation of dieback thresholds under varying deforestation rates while holding fire feedback and drought cycles constant, directly testing the hypothesis's causal claim.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published field studies on Amazon forest resilience and tipping points (e.g., from Science, Nature, Global Change Biology) — Synthesizes existing empirical and modeling evidence to assess consensus on the relative importance of deforestation versus fire and drought in driving dieback, identifying gaps and contradictory findings.

C007.subject: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold
C007.object: the cumulative length of consecutive dry days exceeding 120 days per year, with fire feedback only becoming a primary driver when deforestation exceeds 20% of the basin
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold the cumulative length of consecutive dry days exceeding 120 days per year, with fire feedback only becoming a primary driver when deforestation exceeds 20% of the basin]

[PATH:empirical] Long-term satellite-based precipitation and dry spell analysis (e.g., TRMM, GPM, CHIRPS) combined with vegetation indices (e.g., NDVI, EVI) over the Amazon basin, focusing on regions with >120 consecutive dry days per year. — Directly tests whether observed dieback correlates with cumulative dry-day length as the primary driver, and whether fire feedback becomes dominant only above 20% deforestation.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic global vegetation model (DGVM) experiments, such as LPJmL or INLAND, that simulate Amazon forest response under varying scenarios of dry-day length and deforestation extent, isolating fire feedback effects. — Allows controlled testing of the hypothesized threshold interactions and the 20% deforestation switch for fire feedback dominance, providing mechanistic confirmation or refutation.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of empirical studies on Amazon fire frequency and severity (e.g., from MODIS burned area products) in relation to deforestation gradients and dry-season length, focusing on sites with >20% versus <20% basin cover loss. — Synthesizes existing evidence to see if fire feedback consistently emerges as a primary driver only above 20% deforestation, across multiple studies and regions.

C008.subject: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold
C008.object: fire feedback mechanisms, with drought frequency acting as a contributing factor
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Amazon rainforest dieback threshold fire feedback mechanisms, with drought frequency acting as a contributing factor]

[PATH:empirical] Field experiments quantifying fire-induced tree mortality and subsequent flammability feedbacks in the southern Amazon, e.g., the Amazon Fire Experiment (AFEX) or similar large-scale burn plots — Direct observation of fire feedback strength under varying drought conditions can empirically test whether fire thresholds dominate over drought alone in driving dieback.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic global vegetation model (DGVM) simulations that isolate fire feedbacks from drought effects, such as those using LPJ-GUESS or INLAND with explicit fire modules — Controlled modeling experiments can partition the relative contribution of fire feedbacks versus drought frequency to forest collapse, providing theoretical support or refutation of the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Paleoecological reconstructions of Amazon forest response during past periods of intensified drought and fire (e.g., mid-Holocene or last glacial maximum), using charcoal and pollen records — Historical analogs can reveal whether fire feedbacks were the primary driver of past dieback events, informing the proposed mechanism under high-emission scenarios.
